sentences.text: Ornithomimus was a genus of ornithomimid theropod dinosaurs found in western North America during the Late Cretaceous.
This swift, bipedal dinosaur was covered in feathers and superficially resembled ratites, possessing small skulls, light bones, and long necks.
It featured a small toothless beak and bird-like skulls, indicating an omnivorous diet rather than a purely carnivorous one.
The animal had very long limbs and hollow bones, with the tibia approximately 20% longer than the femur, suggesting it was a swift runner.
In 2010, Gregory S. Paul estimated the length of Ornithomimus edmontonicus at 3.8 meters and its weight at 170 kilograms.
A fourth feathered specimen described in October 2015 was the first to preserve tail feathers.
The first fossils were found in 1889 by George Lyman Cannon, and the type species Ornithomimus velox was named in 1890 by Othniel Charles Marsh.
Marsh based this name on a partial hindlimb and forelimb discovered on June 30, 1889.
The generic name means "bird imitator," derived from Greek ornis and mimos, referring to the bird-like foot.

The diet of Ornithomimus is debated; while theropods might have been carnivorous, its body shape suggests a largely omnivorous lifestyle eating leaves, fruits, small mammals, reptiles, shellfish, insects, and eggs.
Large eye sockets suggest Ornithomimus had a keen visual sense and possibly lived nocturnally.
A 2001 study by Bruce Rothschild and others examined 178 Ornithomimus foot bones for stress fractures but found none.
Starting in 1995, several specimens preserving feather evidence were found, with a 2012 study concluding adults had moderate wing structures likely used for mating displays.
Ornithomimus is usually classified into two species: Ornithomimus velox and Ornithomimus edmontonicus, with the latter being the type species.
Gregory S. Paul classified several genera including Archaeornithomimus, Struthiomimus, Dromiceiomimus, and Gallimimus as species of Ornithomimus in 1988, though this view is not widely accepted.
Marsh initially thought Ornithomimus was an ornithopod, but this changed after Hatcher found a partial ornithomimid skeleton in Wyoming, which Marsh named O. sedens in 1892.
Ornithomimus lived during the Campanian to Maastrichtian ages of the Late Cretaceous, between 83.6 and 66 million years ago.
It lived during the late Cretaceous, approximately 70 to 66 million years ago in the Maastrichtian stage, in what is now North America.
It is debated whether Coelosaurus antiquus belongs to Ornithomimus, with some researchers considering it a nomen dubium.
A 2010 re-evaluation by Lindsay Zanno and colleagues cast doubt on the assignment of a Kaiparowits Formation specimen to O. velox and possibly even to Ornithomimus.

In 1920, Charles Whitney Gilmore named O. affinis for Dryosaurus grandis based on indeterminate material, a classification that is now considered dubious, and in 1933, William Arthur Parks created O. elegans, which is now seen as belonging to Chirostenotes or Elmisaurus.
